hook.line: Tomás is in bed with the flu, and Vale keeps phoning to tell him how relaxed she is. Four times a day. Here's how to say *not at all*, and *too much*.

examples.es: La sopa no es muy rica.
El examen no fue nada fácil.
examples.en: The exam wasn't easy at all.

examples.es: Don Hernando no está nada tranquilo.
examples.en: Don Hernando isn't calm at all.

rule:
Four ways to grade an adjective, from fact to complaint:
*muy caro*: very expensive. Just a fact.
*demasiado caro*: too expensive. More than you want, so it's always a complaint.
*no es muy caro*: not very expensive. A soft verdict.
*no es nada caro*: not expensive at all. Strong.
English puts *at all* at the end. Spanish puts *nada* right before the adjective and keeps *no* before the verb.
*Demasiado* and *nada* never change. Only the adjective agrees: *demasiado caras*, *nada preocupada*.
smallPrint: Teachers call *muy*, *demasiado* and *nada* in this spot degree words, or intensifiers. Here *demasiado* works as an adverb, which is why it never takes *-a* or *-s*.

readAndPick.es: La clase no es nada interesante.
options: The class isn't interesting at all.

readAndPick.es: El hotel no es muy bonito.
options: The hotel isn't nice at all.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick *muy* or *demasiado* and type the whole sentence. It's a complaint: you can't pay it. *El arriendo es ___ caro.*
yourTurn.why: More than you want is *demasiado*. *Muy caro* would just be a fact.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick *muy* or *nada* and type the whole sentence: *El examen no es ___ fácil.* (The exam isn't easy at all.)
yourTurn.answer: El examen no es nada fácil.
yourTurn.why: *At all* is *nada*, right before the adjective.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: The apartment is too small.
yourTurn.why: Too small is a complaint, so *demasiado*.

yourTurn.prompt: Give a soft verdict: The hotel isn't very nice.
yourTurn.answer: El hotel no es muy bonito.
yourTurn.why: *No es muy* is the gentle way to criticise.

yourTurn.prompt: A woman speaking: I'm not worried at all.
yourTurn.why: *Nada* goes right before the adjective, and *preocupada* ends in *-a* because a woman is speaking.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it stronger: *La película no es muy larga.*
yourTurn.answer: La película no es nada larga.
yourTurn.why: Swap *muy* for *nada* and the soft verdict becomes a strong one.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it plural: *La camisa es demasiado cara.*
yourTurn.why: The adjective goes plural, but *demasiado* stays exactly as it is.

pitfalls.why: Close. Before an adjective, *demasiado* never changes. Only *caras* agrees.
Careful. *Demasiado* is always a complaint, so this sounds like a problem. For praise, use *muy*.
English puts *at all* at the end. Spanish puts *nada* right before the adjective.

personal: Give two quick verdicts on your own life: one thing that is *demasiado* something (your rent, your commute, your phone) and one thing that *no es nada* something.
